Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease
  • Source: Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Vol. 26 (2026)
  • Topic: Alcohol-associated liver disease diagnosis, management, and transplantation
  • Author(s): Lee BP, Maddur H, Arab JP, Louvet A
1. Epidemiology & Trends
  • ALD is the leading cause of liver-related mortality in Western countries
  • Deaths attributed to ALD projected to increase by 2040
  • COVID-19 pandemic fueled rise in cases of advanced liver disease
  • Dramatic rise in alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) during pandemic era
  • Rates of heavy alcohol consumption sustained post-pandemic
1.1 Demographic Shifts
  • Liver disease rates ↑ among ages 25–34
  • Narrowing gender gap: women increasingly affected by ALD
  • Survey data shows ↑ rates of excessive drinking among women
  • Women have ↓ referral and transplant rates vs men
1.2 Disparities & Access
  • Black patients and socially vulnerable populations face ↓ access to care
  • Insurance status, physician bias, income disparities impact referral → listing
  • Early LT for AH shows particularly evident disparities
1.3 Public Health Interventions
  • Non-traditional screening settings (e.g., public venues)
  • Policy proposals: ↑ alcohol taxation, ↓ availability, marketing regulations
2. MetALD & Metabolic Overlap
  • Multisociety Delphi consensus created "MetALD" subcategory of steatotic liver disease
  • MetALD = overlap between ALD and metabolic dysfunction-associated liver disease (MASLD)
  • Classification based on metabolic cofactors + alcohol quantity consumed
2.1 Diagnostic Thresholds
  • ALD: >30–60 g/day (men), >20–50 g/day (women)
  • MetALD: intermediate alcohol intake + metabolic risk factors
  • Heavy alcohol + obesity/metabolic syndrome → ↑ cirrhosis rates
2.2 Cardiometabolic Risk Factors
  • Impair recompensation even with alcohol abstinence
  • Contribute to disease progression in ALD
2.3 Genetic Factors
  • PNPLA3 rs738409: major genetic risk factor for ALD
  • Protective alleles: HSDB713, FAF2 (decreased ALD susceptibility in certain populations)
  • These genes now targets of clinical trials for treatment modification
3. Diagnosis: Serum-Based Markers & Tests
3.1 Traditional Serum Markers
  • AST/ALT ratio >2: characteristic of ALD (reflects mitochondrial injury from ethanol)
  • AST/ALT ratio >1: sensitivity 81.3%, specificity 55.3% for cirrhosis
  • AST/ALT ratio >1.5 + acute jaundice/coagulopathy/decompensation → supports AH diagnosis
  • GGT: frequently ↑ from alcohol-induced microsomal enzyme induction (poor specificity)
  • MCV: may reflect direct ethanol toxicity on erythropoiesis/vitamin B12 metabolism
  • Thrombocytopenia: can reflect alcohol-induced bone marrow suppression → artificially inflate FIB-4
3.2 Phosphatidylethanol (PEth)
  • Direct phospholipid metabolite of ethanol in erythrocyte membranes
  • Outperforms GGT/MCV for detecting sustained alcohol use
3.2.1 Diagnostic Thresholds
  • ≥200 ng/mL: regular high-level intake consistent with ALD
  • 20–35 ng/mL: supports MetALD diagnosis
3.2.2 Clinical Utility
  • 3–4× higher detection of ALD/MetALD vs self-report alone
  • Independently predicts progression to cirrhosis and liver-related mortality
  • Longitudinal monitoring enables objective abstinence verification
3.3 Serum-Based Non-Invasive Tests (NITs)
3.3.1 FIB-4 Index
  • Formula: age, AST, ALT, platelet count
  • Sensitivity ~70%, specificity 97% for advanced fibrosis
  • First-line triage tool in clinical practice
  • Caveat: AST elevation + thrombocytopenia from bone marrow suppression → inflated scores independent of true fibrosis
3.3.2 Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) Test
  • Components: hyaluronic acid, PIIINP, TIMP-1
  • Directly reflects extracellular matrix remodeling
  • AUROC 0.92 for advanced fibrosis, 0.94 for cirrhosis
  • Sensitivity 79%, specificity 91%
  • Outperforms FIB-4 and indirect markers in ALD
  • Serial ELF independently predicts decompensation and liver-related mortality
3.3.3 Pro-C3 / ADAPT Algorithm
  • Type III procollagen neoepitope (generated during active fibrogenesis)
  • ADAPT: age, diabetes status, platelet count, type IV collagen
  • Correlates with histological fibrosis severity more strongly than indirect markers
  • Responsive to treatment → candidate pharmacodynamic endpoint in antifibrotic trials
  • Needs further multiethnic validation
4. Elastography & Imaging-Based Assessment
4.1 Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography (VCTE)
  • Most widely validated imaging-based method for ALD fibrosis staging
  • Provides quantitative liver stiffness measurements (LSM)
4.1.1 Validated Cutoffs
  • ≥F3 fibrosis: 12.1 kPa (AUROC 0.90)
  • Cirrhosis: 18.6 kPa (AUROC 0.91)
  • <8–10 kPa: high negative predictive value for excluding advanced fibrosis
4.1.2 ALD-Specific Caveats
  • Hepatic inflammation, steatohepatitis, cholestasis → overestimates LSM independently of fibrosis
  • AST >200 IU/L or elevated bilirubin: significant overestimation risk
  • Reassess after abstinence: LSM may decline >20% within 2–4 weeks
  • Serial change ≥20% predicts decompensation events and liver-related mortality
4.2 Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP)
  • Measured simultaneously with VCTE
  • Point-of-care quantification of hepatic steatosis
  • Provides complementary phenotypic information across steatotic liver disease spectrum
4.3 Two-Dimensional Shear-Wave Elastography (2D-SWE)
  • Small studies with variable performance
  • Cutoffs: 10.2 kPa (significant fibrosis, Ishak ≥3), 16.4 kPa (cirrhosis, Ishak ≥5)
  • AUROC >0.92 for both endpoints
4.4 Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE)
  • Highest diagnostic accuracy among available modalities
  • Sensitivity 96%, specificity 95% for advanced fibrosis
  • Combined with MRI-PDFF: simultaneous assessment of fibrosis and steatosis
4.4.1 Indications
  • VCTE technically limited or intermediate results
  • Obesity, ascites, narrow intercostal spaces
  • Serial imaging for monitoring without radiation exposure
5. Practical Sequential Diagnostic Approach
5.1 Recommended Algorithm
  • Initial encounter: PEth + standard liver biochemistry panel + FIB-4
  • Simultaneous objective alcohol documentation and first-line fibrosis risk stratification
5.2 Next Steps for Elevated FIB-4
  • Proceed to ELF testing or VCTE for refined staging
  • Explicitly consider ALD-specific confounders:
  • Active hepatic inflammation
  • Recent alcohol use
5.3 Reassessment Criteria
  • Elevated aminotransferases at initial elastography → reassess LSM after abstinence
  • Liver biopsy reserved for:
  • Discordant non-invasive results
  • Unresolved diagnostic uncertainty between competing etiologies
  • Histological confirmation of AH when clinical/biochemical criteria insufficient
5.4 Future Integration
  • Genetic risk markers (PNPLA3 rs738409, polygenic risk scores) may refine long-term stratification
  • Distinguish genetic ancestry from self-identified race/ethnicity
6. Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis (AH)
6.1 Definition & Terminology
  • EASL definition: "AH" = clinical manifestations related to alcohol-induced inflammation
  • ASH (alcohol-associated steatohepatitis) = histological diagnosis
  • Discordance between clinical signs (jaundice) and liver histology is common
6.2 Epidemiology
  • Incidence ↑ in North America, especially during COVID-19 pandemic
  • More stable in European countries (e.g., Denmark)
  • Difficult to estimate due to ICD coding uncertainties
6.3 Clinical Presentation
  • Heavy alcohol intake: ~100–200 g/day (10 international units)
  • Can develop with lower amounts
  • Cardinal symptom: recent onset of jaundice without identifiable alternative cause
6.4 Biological Features
  • Moderately elevated transaminases with AST/ALT ratio >1
  • Hyperbilirubinemia (predominantly conjugated)
  • Prolonged prothrombin time or elevated INR
  • Most patients have underlying cirrhosis → clinical signs (ascites, encephalopathy, spider naevi)
  • Biological signs of chronic alcohol consumption: ↑IgA, ↑MCV
6.5 Diagnostic Confirmation
  • Liver biopsy ideal (often transjugular due to coagulopathy/ascites)
  • Non-invasive criteria proposed by experts (need refinement)
6.5.1 Histological Features
  • Polymorphonuclear neutrophil infiltration
  • Ballooned hepatocytes
  • Mallory-Denk bodies
  • Variable fibrosis and steatosis (dependent on duration of alcohol use, time since last drink)
  • Histological features predict outcomes
6.6 Infectious Complications
  • ~30% of patients admitted with AH have evidence of infection on systematic screening
  • Most frequent: lung infections, UTI, bacteremia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
6.6.1 Systematic Screening (Upon Admission)
  • Blood cultures
  • Urinalysis
  • Ascites fluid examination
  • Chest X-ray (chest CT preferred in high-risk: encephalopathy, tobacco exposure, high MELD score)
6.6.2 Clinical Reasoning
  • Sequence of events crucial: infection vs AH as primary precipitant
  • Jaundice first → fever later = more likely AH with secondary infection
  • Simultaneous jaundice + fever = less likely pure AH
6.7 ACLF Relationship
  • Most AH patients have underlying cirrhosis or extensive fibrosis → acute event on chronic liver disease
  • ACLF precipitated by infection, GI bleeding, AH, or other conditions
  • High proportion of AH patients meet ACLF criteria
  • ACLF-2 or 3: highest short-term mortality
  • Grade 3 ACLF: probability of response to corticosteroids <10% → early LT evaluation preferred
7. Pharmacological Treatment of Severe AH
7.1 Corticosteroids: Primary Therapy
  • Prednisolone 40 mg/day for 28 days (EASL and AASLD guidelines)
  • Benefit confirmed by meta-analyses with/without individual patient data
7.1.1 Patient Selection
  • Maddrey's discriminant function (DF) >32 → inclusion criterion in RCTs
  • MELD score superior to DF for predicting outcome (used in practice)
  • MELD 20–40: most significant survival benefit from corticosteroids
  • MELD >25–40: optimal impact on survival
7.1.2 Response Assessment: Lille Model
  • Calculated after 7-day corticosteroid course
  • Variables: age, prothrombin time, albumin, renal insufficiency, bilirubin (day 0 and day 7)
  • Lille <0.45: responders → continue treatment
  • Lille ≥0.56: non-responders → stop steroids, consider alternative
7.1.3 Survival Outcomes
  • Short-term (28-day) survival improved by corticosteroids
  • No improvement at 3 or 6 months → not ideal treatment
  • Meta-analysis: prednisolone should be stopped after 7 days if Lille ≥0.56
7.1.4 Infection Risk
  • Meta-analysis: no ↑ infection risk vs placebo (when controlling for occult infections)
  • STOPAH trial: more infections in steroid-treated patients (mostly pneumonia)
  • Lack of systematic infection screening at admission → may have led to steroid administration in occult infections
  • Opportunistic infections: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, aspergillosis
7.2 Alternative Agents (All Failed to Improve Survival)
  • N-acetylcysteine + corticosteroids
  • Pentoxifylline
  • Enteral nutrition
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate (prophylactic)
  • Anakinra (IL-1 antagonist) vs prednisolone
7.3 Promising Investigational Agents
  • Larsucosterol (sulfated oxysterol, immune modulator)
  • F-652 (IL-22 agonist)
7.4 Post-Treatment Course
  • Responders: continue prednisolone 40 mg/day for 1 month → discontinue (with or without tapering)
  • Hepatic improvement over subsequent months
  • Significant proportion still exhibit impaired liver function despite abstinence + treatment
7.5 Long-Term Outcomes & AUD Treatment
  • Return to drinking does not affect short-term (6-month) survival after AH episode
  • Strongly impacts long-term outcome → integrated care essential
7.5.1 Engagement Gap
  • Pharmacological treatment for AUD remains low in cirrhosis patients
  • Must be improved
8. Liver Transplantation for ALD
8.1 Current Landscape
  • ALD surpassed HCV as leading indication for LT in US (2016)
  • Largest number of waitlist registrations and transplants currently
  • Shift toward younger adults and women now evident in transplant population
8.2 Early Transplantation for Severe AH
  • Traditional requirement: 6-month fixed abstinence interval (1983 NIH consensus suggestion)
  • Lacked firm evidentiary basis
  • Poorly suited to severe AH where corticosteroid non-response → 70–80% 6-month mortality
8.2.1 Historical Evidence
  • Mathurin et al. (2011): first publication of early LT concept
  • Highly selected: first-episode, corticosteroid-nonresponsive patients
  • Represented <2% of those screened
  • 6-month survival: 77% vs 23% in matched non-transplanted patients
  • Benefit persisted at 2 years
  • Return to alcohol use: infrequent
8.2.2 Subsequent Studies (Table 3)
  • ACCELERATE-AH cohort (147 patients, 12 US centers):
  • 94% at 1 year, 84% at 3 years
  • Any alcohol use: 25% (1 year), 34% (3 years)
  • Sustained use: ~10% (1 year), 17% (3 years)
  • QuickTrans study (prospective, controlled):
  • Substantial survival advantage for early LT over standard care
  • Return to alcohol use documented in sizable minority
  • Meta-analysis (~6,000 patients across 42 studies):
  • 89% at 1 year, 78% at 5 years
  • No significant difference between early and standard LT
8.2.3 Living Donor LT
  • Offered at small number of centers with established programs
  • Experience limited; role relative to deceased-donor early LT not yet defined
8.3 Candidate Selection
  • Shifted from elapsed time to structured psychosocial evaluation
8.3.1 Favorable Features
  • First episode of hepatic decompensation
  • Insight into diagnosis
  • Stable support network
  • Absence of severe psychiatric illness or co-occurring substance use disorder
8.3.2 SALT Score (Sustained Alcohol Use Post-LT)
  • Derived from ACCELERATE-AH cohort
  • Range: 0–11 points
Variable Points
>10 drinks/day at initial AH hospitalization +4
Multiple formal rehabilitation attempts +4
Alcohol-related legal issues (e.g., DUI arrest) +2
Prior illicit substance use +1
  • Score <5: high negative predictive value for sustained use
  • Most useful for identifying low-risk candidates
  • Caution against using to exclude patients
8.3.3 Dallas Consensus Framework
  • Protocolized pathways for expedited evaluation
  • Single-system implementation → favorable survival with low return to alcohol use
8.3.4 Dynamic Reassessment
  • ~20% of patients referred for early LT achieve spontaneous recovery without transplant
  • Timing and dynamic reassessment crucial (minority of patients)
8.4 Disparities in Access to Early LT
  • Proportion of transplants for AH varies several-fold across centers/regions
  • Reflects differences in local practice and case mix
  • Social determinants of health associated with ↓ referral → listing progression:
  • Medicaid insurance
  • Neighborhood-level social vulnerability
8.4.1 Evaluation Barriers
  • Stable housing, transportation, identified caregiver = standard psychosocial requirements
  • Harder to demonstrate for patients with fewer resources
8.4.2 Addiction Specialist Access
  • Limited outside larger academic centers (before and after transplant)
8.5 Alcohol Use After Transplantation
8.5.1 Clinical Distinction
  • Any alcohol use: common, usually does not compromise graft
  • Sustained or harmful use: associated with recurrent steatohepatitis, accelerated fibrosis, graft loss, reduced long-term survival
8.5.2 Biomarker Monitoring
  • Self-report underestimates use → many programs incorporate PEth
  • More sensitive detection than history alone
8.5.3 Reabstinence Benefit
  • Multicenter analysis: recipients achieving reabstinence after harmful use:
  • 5-year survival: 94% (vs 93% with no harmful use)
  • Substantially higher than those with continued harmful use (77%)
  • Harmful use after transplant = modifiable determinant of outcome
8.5.4 Retransplantation
  • Uncommon and ethically contested in setting of return to alcohol use
9. Treatment of Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD)
9.1 Pharmacotherapy in Advanced Liver Disease & Post-LT
9.1.1 Acamprosate
  • Clearance: renal (no hepatic metabolism)
  • Dose reduction needed for renal impairment (common post-LT)
  • Main side effect: diarrhea
  • No interaction with tacrolimus or cyclosporine → often first choice
  • Evidence: pilot RCT post-LT showed safety/tolerability; observational data in cirrhosis suggest benefit
9.1.2 Naltrexone
  • Clearance: hepatic
  • Blocks opioid analgesia → held around surgery time
  • Older hepatotoxicity concern not borne out at standard doses
  • Few data in decompensated disease
  • Evidence: mostly extrapolated from general AUD trials; small series in cirrhosis
9.1.3 Baclofen
  • Clearance: renal
  • Sedation and confusion at higher doses → precipitates encephalopathy concern
  • Dose adjust for renal function
  • Evidence: RCT in cirrhosis showed higher abstinence rates; general AUD results mixed
9.1.4 Gabapentin
  • Clearance: renal
  • Most useful when withdrawal symptoms prominent
  • Side effects: sedation, some misuse potential
  • Dose adjust for renal function
  • Evidence: RCT in general AUD population; no dedicated data in cirrhosis/post-LT
9.1.5 Topiramate
  • Clearance: mostly renal
  • Side effects: cognitive slowing, paresthesias, metabolic acidosis, kidney stones
  • Evidence: general AUD trials only
9.1.6 Semaglutide / GLP-1 Receptor Agonists
  • Clearation: proteolytic
  • Concerns in decompensated patients: weight loss, nausea (already sarcopenic)
  • Slowed gastric emptying → may change immunosuppressant absorption
  • Not recommended outside of trial at present
  • Evidence: small phase 2 RCT in non-treatment-seeking adults with AUD; observational cohorts linking GLP-1 to fewer alcohol-related outcomes
  • No prospective data in cirrhosis or post-LT
9.1.7 Disulfiram
  • Not included due to hepatotoxicity → generally avoided in cirrhosis and post-LT
9.2 Behavioral Interventions
  • Most effective when combined with pharmacotherapy
  • Components: motivational interviewing, cognitive behavioral therapy, structured counseling
9.2.1 Delivery Setting
  • Delivered within hepatology and transplant settings (not external referral)
  • Randomized evidence supports embedding addiction specialists within transplant team
9.3 Clinical Outcomes
  • AUD treatment in patients with cirrhosis → lower rates of decompensation and death
  • Integrated models (hepatology + addiction care concurrently) increasingly regarded as standard
9.4 Post-Transplant Care Model
  • Single-center program with integrated addiction treatment → low rates of return to alcohol use
9.5 Relapse Management
  • AUD is a chronic, treatable condition
  • Return to alcohol use after transplant → reassessment and escalation of treatment (not withdrawal of care)
